ELSA: Exact Linear-Scan Attention for Fast and Memory-Light
Vision Transformers

Chih-Chung Hsu    Xin-Di Ma    Wo-Ting Liao    Chia-Ming Lee Affiliation: Advanced Computer Vision Laboratory, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
Abstract

Existing attention accelerators often trade exact softmax semantics, depend on fused Tensor Core kernels, or incur sequential depth that limits FP32 throughput on long sequences. We present ELSA, an algorithmic reformulation of online softmax attention that (i) preserves exact softmax semantics in real arithmetic with a provable 𝒪⁡(u​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(u\log n) FP32 relative error bound; (ii) casts the online softmax update as a prefix scan over an associative monoid (m,S,W)(m,S,W), yielding O⁡(n)O(n) extra memory and O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) parallel depth; and (iii) is Tensor-Core independent, implemented in Triton and CUDA C++, and deployable as a drop-in replacement requiring no retraining or weight modification. Unlike FlashAttention-2/3, which rely on HMMA/GMMA Tensor Core instructions and provide no compatible FP32 path, ELSA operates identically on A100s and resource-constrained edge devices such as Jetson TX2—making it the only hardware-agnostic exact-attention kernel that reduces parallel depth to O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) at full precision. On A100 FP32 benchmarks (1K–16K tokens), ELSA delivers 1.31.3–3.5×3.5\times speedup over memory-efficient SDPA and 1.971.97–2.27×2.27\times on BERT; on Jetson TX2, ELSA achieves 1.51.5–1.6×1.6\times over Math (64–900 tokens), with 17.817.8–20.2%20.2\% throughput gains under LLaMA-13B offloading at ≥\geq32K. In FP16, ELSA approaches hardware-fused baselines at long sequences while retaining full FP32 capability, offering a unified kernel for high-precision inference across platforms. Our code and implementation are available at https://github.com/ming053l/ELSA.

1 Introduction

Vision Transformers (ViT) [37, 11] have achieved remarkable success across computer vision, but their Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) suffers from quadratic memory scaling. A 4K image (4096×40964096\times 4096), tokenized at a 4×44{\times}4 patch size typical of high-resolution scientific models, yields ≈1​M{\approx}1\text{M} tokens and requires over 4 TB of GPU memory to materialize the full attention matrix in FP32—far exceeding commercial hardware capacity. This 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) bottleneck is particularly critical in high-precision domains such as medical imaging, hyperspectral analysis, and super-resolution microscopy, where FP32 accuracy is non-negotiable [12, 48, 44, 21, 9]. Accelerating attention while preserving exactness and precision is thus essential for scaling ViTs to high-resolution applications.

Challenges. Existing approaches remain limited for high-speed, high-precision inference. Current strategies fall into three paradigms: approximate attention [4, 40, 46], which linearize complexity via low-rank projections or sparse patterns; hardware-fused kernels like FlashAttention-2/3 [8, 33], which achieve linear memory through block-tiling and Tensor Core instructions; and memory-efficient implementations such as ME-SDPA [5], which reduce memory via sequential computation. Each faces critical limitations: approximate methods alter the attention operator, requiring retraining that is infeasible for foundation models trained over millions of GPU hours and cost-intensive data curation (e.g., CLIP [30], SAM [18], LLaMA [36], and 3D Large Reconstruction Model like VGGT [39]); FlashAttention’s FP32 path reverts to untuned SIMD without fused HMMA kernels and requires per-generation tuning; ME-SDPA, despite supporting FP32, suffers 𝒪⁡(n/Tk)\mathcal{O}(n/T_{k}) sequential depth—3.5×3.5\times slower than ELSA at 16K tokens. We therefore restrict comparisons to exact drop-in implementations (Math kernel, ME-SDPA, FA2/FA3); approximate methods fall outside fair evaluation scope as they require retraining every benchmark model.

Problem Formulation. What remains missing is an exact, inherently parallel reformulation of attention that requires no specialized hardware. The online softmax recurrence of Rabe and Staats [29] reduces memory to 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) but remains inherently sequential. For the ≈1​M{\approx}1\text{M}-token 4K example above, a GPU must synchronize over one million steps, leaving pipelines idle. Breaking this sequential bottleneck is the key challenge for efficient FP32 attention.

To address this, we propose Exact Linear-Scan Attention (ELSA), which reformulates the online softmax recurrence as a prefix scan over an associative monoid, achieving 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log n) parallel depth and 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) memory with exact FP32 semantics, no retraining, and no Tensor Core dependency (in FP32 we provide a provable bound under Assumption 1). Table 1 summarizes how ELSA uniquely combines exactness, FP32 efficiency, and GPU-agnostic design. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    Provable FP32 error bound and deployable kernel. We formalize the online softmax merge operator ⊕\oplus on state triples (m,S,W)∈ℝ¯×ℝ≥0×ℝdv(m,S,W)\!\in\!\bar{\mathbb{R}}\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} as a monoid—going beyond prior theoretical treatments [13] by proving closure, associativity, and identity—and derive a kernel-aware 𝒪⁡(u​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(u\log n)11 1 We write uu for FP32 unit roundoff; FP64 would be denoted by u64u_{64}. FP32 relative error bound tied to scan merge depth, enabling provable numerical stability for million-token sequences on real hardware.

  • •

    Hardware-agnostic implementation. We implement a two-level scan (intra-block Hillis–Steele, inter-block Blelloch) in Triton and CUDA C++ without Tensor Core dependencies, achieving high-throughput FP32 inference across platforms from data-centre GPUs (e.g., A100, L4) to embedded devices (Jetson TX2).

  • •

    Retraining-free deployment. ELSA preserves exact softmax semantics as a drop-in replacement for pretrained large foundation models, such as CLIP, ViT, LLaMA, and VGGT, enabling immediate acceleration without fine-tuning, which is critical for foundation models trained over millions of GPU hours.

  • •

    Comprehensive evaluation. Across vision and language benchmarks, (i) in FP32 ELSA improves latency over memory-efficient SDPA by 1.31.3–3.5×3.5\times while using comparable peak memory; (ii) in FP16 ELSA approaches FlashAttention-2/3 throughput at long sequences while achieving the lowest peak memory among exact kernels (e.g., 0.190.19 GB vs. 0.290.29/0.360.36 GB at 16K, Figure 4). (iii) under host-device offloading, ELSA delivers 17.8–20.2% throughput gains over ME-SDPA at ≥\geq32K tokens (LLaMA-13B, FP32).

2 Related Works

Attention Approximation. A major research branch approximates the attention matrix to achieve 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) complexity, but at the cost of modifying the attention operator itself. Performer [4] applies random feature maps to linearize the exponential kernel, replacing exact softmax with a kernel approximation that enables linear-time computation but introduces approximation error. Linformer [40] projects keys and values to a lower-dimensional space via learned linear projections, reducing the effective sequence length but losing full token-to-token interactions. Sparse attention methods such as BigBird [46] and Sparse Transformers [3] restrict attention to predefined patterns (e.g., local windows, random connections, global tokens), discarding most pairwise interactions to achieve sparsity. Nyströmformer [43] approximates the attention matrix via the Nyström method using landmark tokens, and Reformer [19] employs locality-sensitive hashing to cluster similar queries and keys. More recently, DeltaNet [38] parallelizes linear Transformers with the delta rule over sequence length using a hardware-efficient chunk-wise scan, achieving 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) training complexity while retaining recurrent expressiveness. While these methods achieve attractive theoretical complexity, they inevitably modify the attention operator and require training a model from scratch to compensate for the approximation—impractical for foundation models such as CLIP [30] or SAM [18] trained over millions of GPU hours and labour-intensive data curation. In contrast, ELSA preserves exact softmax semantics and serves as a drop-in replacement without any retraining.

Hardware-fused Attention. FlashAttention-2 (FA2) [8] pioneered tiling attention to fit on-chip memory, achieving linear memory use and 22–4×4\times speedups by fusing Q​K⊤QK^{\top}, softmax, and VV within shared memory using 16×1616{\times}16 tiles aligned to Tensor Core (HMMA) instructions. FlashAttention-3 (FA3) [33] further improves throughput via finer tile partitioning and warp-specialization. Both kernels, however, depend critically on HMMA/GMMA instructions optimized for FP16/BF16; without them, execution reverts to SIMD paths and the throughput advantage largely disappears. Both are also tightly coupled to specific GPU generations, complicating deployment on older or embedded devices.

The Case for Exact FP32 Attention. Despite the prevalence of BF16/FP16, FP32 remains indispensable in several settings: hyperspectral imaging, where 12–16-bit sensor dynamic range is irrecoverable under half-precision accumulation [50, 17]; medical image analysis, where clinical accuracy requirements preclude any approximation [12, 21]; zero-shot deployment of foundation models (CLIP [30], SAM [18], and VGGT [39]), where retraining to recalibrate precision-induced drift is infeasible; and mixed-precision pipelines that require a numerically auditable FP32 attention sub-module. In all these cases, FA2/FA3’s FP32 path is uncompetitive and ME-SDPA’s sequential depth imposes a 3.5×3.5\times latency penalty at 16K tokens. ELSA addresses this gap by treating softmax as an algorithmic problem: an associative monoid over (m,S,W)(m,S,W) solved via prefix-scan, delivering exact, high-throughput FP32 inference across platforms, from A100s to Jetson devices, without any Tensor Core dependency.

Efficient Memory and Architecture Design. Beyond approximation and hardware fusion, a parallel line of work reduces memory through architectural redesign. In distributed settings, DistFlashAttn [22] overlaps compute and communication to extend FA2 across devices. In vision, representative designs include EfficientViT’s cascaded group attention [24], ELFATT’s sparse-blockify approach [42], SHViT’s single-head design [45], L2ViT’s information concentration [49], and META’s cross-shaped window attention [47]. While these designs achieve efficiency through structural modifications, they require task-specific retraining and cannot serve as drop-in replacements for pretrained models.

Most closely related to ELSA are three lines of work. Feng et al. [13] identify that the online softmax recurrence admits parallel prefix reduction, but neither formalize it as a monoid nor deliver a deployable FP32 kernel with a quantitative error bound. LeanAttention [32] exploits associativity only for single-query decode. ME-SDPA [5] preserves exact FP32 semantics but processes tokens sequentially, incurring 𝒪⁡(n/Tk)\mathcal{O}(n/T_{k}) depth and a 3.5×3.5\times latency penalty at 16K tokens. ELSA addresses all three gaps: (i) a triple-state monoid (m,S,W)(m,S,W) with formally proven closure, associativity, and identity; (ii) all-queries (prefill) attention; and (iii) a provable FP32 error bound tied to scan depth L⁡(n,B)L(n,B)—making ELSA a general, training-free, numerically auditable drop-in for vision and language inference.

3 Motivation and Preliminaries

Efficient attention requires addressing two intertwined challenges: the 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) memory cost of materializing the full score matrix, and the sequential depth of memory-efficient implementations that avoid it. We first characterize the sequential bottleneck and then introduce the parallel prefix scan framework that ELSA exploits to overcome it.

3.1 Why Is Sequential Attention a Bottleneck?

Self-attention and Quadratic Memory.

Given a sequence of nn tokens, let qi,kj∈ℝdq_{i},k_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the query and key vectors and vj∈ℝdvv_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} the value vector. The attention score si​j=⟨qi,kj⟩/ds_{ij}=\langle q_{i},k_{j}\rangle/\sqrt{d} and output are

yi=∑jesi​j​vj∑jesi​j.y_{i}=\frac{\sum_{j}e^{s_{ij}}v_{j}}{\sum_{j}e^{s_{ij}}}. (1)

Naive materialization of the full n×nn{\times}n score matrix requires 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) memory, which becomes prohibitive at long sequence lengths. To avoid this, one instead maintains a running state (mj,Sj,Wj)(m_{j},S_{j},W_{j}), where mj=maxu≤j⁡sum_{j}=\max_{u\leq j}s_{u} is the running maximum logit, Sj=∑u=1jesu−mjS_{j}=\sum_{u=1}^{j}e^{s_{u}-m_{j}} the normalized cumulative sum, and Wj=∑u=1jesu−mj​vuW_{j}=\sum_{u=1}^{j}e^{s_{u}-m_{j}}v_{u} the corresponding weighted sum, reducing memory to 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) without storing intermediate scores.

Online Softmax Recurrence and Its Sequential Depth.

Rabe and Staats [29] showed this 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n)-memory computation can be performed in a single forward sweep via

mj=max⁡(mj−1,sj),Sj=Sj−1​emj−1−mj+esj−mj,Wj=Wj−1​emj−1−mj+esj−mj​vj.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} m_{j}&=\max(m_{j-1},\,s_{j}),\\ S_{j}&=S_{j-1}\,e^{m_{j-1}-m_{j}}+e^{s_{j}-m_{j}},\\ W_{j}&=W_{j-1}\,e^{m_{j-1}-m_{j}}+e^{s_{j}-m_{j}}\,v_{j}.\end{aligned}

 (2)

Heinsen [14] later proposed a constant-cost-per-token variant confirming the same memory property. However, both formulations are inherently sequential: each step depends on the previous, so a GPU must synchronize nn times, leaving most threads idle. This 𝒪⁡(n/Tk)\mathcal{O}(n/T_{k}) sequential depth in memory-efficient kernels such as ME-SDPA [5] is the core latency bottleneck we address. Throughout, we use exact to mean that our output equals standard softmax attention in real arithmetic; in floating point, we derive a provable FP32 relative error bound (Theorem 1).

3.2 Parallelization via Prefix Scan

Parallel Prefix Scanning.

To overcome the sequential bottleneck, we turn to the theory of parallel prefix scan [1]. A prefix scan computes all prefix reductions over a monoid (⊕,e)(\oplus,e): a set with an associative binary operator and an identity element. Classic algorithms, Hillis–Steele [16], Kogge–Stone [20], and Blelloch’s two-pass [1], achieve 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log n) depth with 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) work. Modern GPU libraries (CUDA CUB, Thrust) generalize these primitives to composite data types: as long as the tuple-level operation is associative and has an identity, prefix scan accumulates vector- or tuple-valued states in parallel without Tensor Core dependencies. This raises a natural question: can the online softmax recurrence be cast as such a monoid? We answer affirmatively in Sec. 4.

Integral-image View of Softmax Attention.

A key obstacle is that each recurrence step depends on the global running maximum mjm_{j}, unknown until all previous tokens are processed. The integral-image view resolves this: just as a 2D integral image lets any rectangular region sum be retrieved in 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) by combining corner values, the attention state over any contiguous block can be recovered by composing the states of its sub-blocks. This composability means blocks can be computed independently in parallel and merged in a logarithmic reduction tree.

Concretely, let sj=⟨q,kj⟩/ds_{j}=\langle q,k_{j}\rangle/\sqrt{d} and mj=maxu≤j⁡sum_{j}=\max_{u\leq j}s_{u}. Define the unnormalized prefix quantities

S~j=∑u≤jesu,W~j=∑u≤jesu​vu,\displaystyle\tilde{S}_{j}=\sum_{u\leq j}e^{s_{u}},\qquad\tilde{W}_{j}=\sum_{u\leq j}e^{s_{u}}\,v_{u},

 (3)

and the normalized state (mj,Sj,Wj)=(mj,S~j​e−mj,W~j​e−mj)(m_{j},S_{j},W_{j})=(m_{j},\,\tilde{S}_{j}e^{-m_{j}},\,\tilde{W}_{j}e^{-m_{j}}). Normalization by e−mje^{-m_{j}}, analogous to the origin correction in integral images, re-anchors accumulated sums to the local maximum, preventing overflow while preserving exact values. The maps un​(m,S,W)=(S​em,W​em)\textsf{un}(m,S,W)=(Se^{m},We^{m}) and renorm​(m,S~,W~)=(m,S~​e−m,W~​e−m)\textsf{renorm}(m,\tilde{S},\tilde{W})=(m,\tilde{S}e^{-m},\tilde{W}e^{-m}) convert between representations; our merge operator ⊕\oplus implements blockwise composition via “un-sum-renorm”, the softmax analogue of summing corner values. This yields a scan over (m,S,W)(m,S,W) in 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log n) depth with 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) extra memory, what we term linear-scan. The key question is whether this blockwise composability can be formalized as a monoid, enabling standard parallel scan primitives. We answer this in Sec. 4; the complete monoid proof and I/O complexity analysis are deferred to the supplementary material.

4 Exact Linear-Scan Attention

Overview.

The integral-image view in Sec. 3 suggests that the online softmax state (m,S,W)(m,S,W) can be composed blockwise (Figure 1); Figure 2 details the three-step merge operator ⊕\oplus that implements this composition. We begin by formalizing this observation.

Proposition 1 (Block composition).

For any partition of indices into contiguous blocks B1,…,BKB_{1},\dots,B_{K}, let u⁡(Bk)u(B_{k}) be the state (m,S,W)(m,S,W) computed on block BkB_{k}. Then u⁡(B1∪⋯∪BK)=u⁡(B1)⊕⋯⊕u⁡(BK)u(B_{1}\cup\cdots\cup B_{K})=u(B_{1})\oplus\cdots\oplus u(B_{K}).

This composability is the foundation of ELSA: because block states can be computed independently in parallel and merged in a logarithmic reduction tree, it suffices to show that ⊕\oplus forms a monoid—thereby admitting standard parallel scan primitives (Sec. 3, Parallel prefix scanning). Unlike LeanAttention [32], which exploits a related property only for single-query decode, our formulation covers all-queries (prefill) attention and provides a formal FP32 error bound tied to scan depth. Similarly, while Feng et al. [13] identify this algebraic structure theoretically, they do not provide a deployable high-throughput FP32 kernel; our contribution lies precisely in this gap.

In this section, we proceed in three steps: (1) proving the monoid structure of ⊕\oplus, (2) deriving the FP32 error bound, and (3) designing the two-level GPU scan.

4.1 Monoid Formulation

Let U=ℝ¯×ℝ≥0×ℝdvU=\bar{\mathbb{R}}\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} with ℝ¯=ℝ∪{−∞}\bar{\mathbb{R}}=\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}, and 𝒆=(−∞,0,𝟎)\boldsymbol{e}=(-\infty,0,\mathbf{0}). The merge operator ⊕\oplus is designed to compose the running states of Eq. (2) blockwise. For ua=(ma,Sa,Wa)u_{a}=(m_{a},S_{a},W_{a}) and ub=(mb,Sb,Wb)u_{b}=(m_{b},S_{b},W_{b}), define

ua⊕ub={(ma,Sa+Sb​emb−ma,Wa+Wb​emb−ma),ma≥mb,(mb,Sb+Sa​ema−mb,Wb+Wa​ema−mb),otherwise.u_{a}\oplus u_{b}=\begin{cases}\bigl(m_{a},\;S_{a}+S_{b}\,e^{m_{b}-m_{a}},\;W_{a}+W_{b}\,e^{m_{b}-m_{a}}\bigr),&m_{a}\geq m_{b},\\[4.0pt] \bigl(m_{b},\;S_{b}+S_{a}\,e^{m_{a}-m_{b}},\;W_{b}+W_{a}\,e^{m_{a}-m_{b}}\bigr),&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

 (4)

Closure. Since emb−ma∈(0,1]e^{m_{b}-m_{a}}\in(0,1] when ma≥mbm_{a}\geq m_{b}, S∈ℝ≥0S\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is preserved and W∈ℝdvW\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} is closed under affine combination; the symmetric case follows by construction.

Associativity. With un​(m,S,W)=(S​em,W​em)\textsf{un}(m,S,W)=(Se^{m},We^{m}) and renorm​(m,S~,W~)=(m,S~​e−m,W~​e−m)\textsf{renorm}(m,\tilde{S},\tilde{W})=(m,\tilde{S}e^{-m},\tilde{W}e^{-m}),

ua⊕ub=renorm​(max⁡(ma,mb),un​(ua)+un​(ub)).\displaystyle u_{a}\oplus u_{b}=\textsf{renorm}\bigl(\max(m_{a},m_{b}),\;\textsf{un}(u_{a})+\textsf{un}(u_{b})\bigr).

 (5)

By associativity of vector addition and max\max, (ua⊕ub)⊕uc=ua⊕(ub⊕uc)(u_{a}\oplus u_{b})\oplus u_{c}=u_{a}\oplus(u_{b}\oplus u_{c}).

Identity. (U,⊕,𝒆)(U,\oplus,\boldsymbol{e}) forms a monoid with identity 𝒆=(−∞,0,𝟎)\boldsymbol{e}=(-\infty,0,\mathbf{0}); a complete proof is given in Supp. A.

4.2 Logical Scan and GPU Parallelization

Logical level. Proposition 1 guarantees that the state (m,S,W)(m,S,W) composes associatively via ⊕\oplus (Eq. (4)), so the full-sequence result equals the sequential prefix product u1⊕⋯⊕unu_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus u_{n}. The per-query sequential formulation (detailed pseudocode and step-by-step explanation in Supp. A.4) makes this explicit: it initializes (m0,S0,W0)=(−∞,0,𝟎)(m_{0},S_{0},W_{0})=(-\infty,0,\mathbf{0}), computes scores, applies the conditional rescaling of Eq. (2), and normalizes. Although the loop is written sequentially, its correctness relies solely on the monoid structure, not on sequential order, which is precisely what enables parallel execution.

Physical level. A naive single-level parallel scan would require all nn threads to synchronize through global memory, incurring high communication overhead at long sequences. ME-SDPA [5] avoids this by processing tiles sequentially, but at the cost of 𝒪⁡(n/Tk)\mathcal{O}(n/T_{k}) depth. FA2/FA3 [8, 33] reduce depth via block tiling, but advance sequentially along the key dimension and depend on Tensor Core fusion unavailable in FP32. To achieve 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log n) depth without these dependencies, we exploit the two-level structure of ⊕\oplus: since ⊕\oplus is associative, blocks can be reduced independently and their results merged in a logarithmic tree. Concretely, since (U,⊕,𝒆)(U,\oplus,\boldsymbol{e}) is a monoid, we map the computation to a two-level prefix scan, choosing algorithms whose properties match each level’s constraints:

  1. 1.

    Intra-block (B=128B=128): Each thread block independently reduces a chunk of 128 tokens via a Hillis–Steele scan [16] in shared memory, contributing ⌈log2⁡B⌉\lceil\log_{2}B\rceil merge levels. Because ⊕\oplus is associative (Sec. 4, Monoid Formulation), any ordering of pairwise merges within the block yields the same result, making Hillis–Steele’s tree-structured reduction provably correct. Hillis–Steele is preferred here because all BB threads remain active throughout every level, maximizing shared-memory bandwidth utilization; at the small block size B=128B{=}128, its 𝒪⁡(B​log⁡B)\mathcal{O}(B\log B) work overhead over the 𝒪⁡(B)\mathcal{O}(B)-optimal alternative is negligible relative to the latency saved by keeping threads busy. Block size B=128B{=}128 balances occupancy and shared-memory usage across GPU generations.

  2. 2.

    Inter-block: A Blelloch two-pass scan [1] aggregates block-level states in global memory, adding 2​⌈log2⁡(n/B)⌉2\lceil\log_{2}(n/B)\rceil merge levels. The identity element 𝒆=(−∞,0,𝟎)\boldsymbol{e}=(-\infty,0,\mathbf{0}) of the monoid enables Blelloch’s down-sweep to initialize boundary states correctly without special-casing empty prefixes. Unlike Hillis–Steele, Blelloch’s up-sweep/down-sweep is work-optimal (𝒪⁡(n/B)\mathcal{O}(n/B) total operations), which is critical at the inter-block level where n/Bn/B can reach the hundreds and unnecessary global memory traffic would dominate latency. The up-sweep computes each block’s total 𝐮tot\mathbf{u}_{\text{tot}}; the down-sweep distributes prefix results back and combines with each block’s internal state via ⊕\oplus, yielding the total depth L⁡(n,B)L(n,B) (Eq. (6)).

4.3 Numerical Stability, Scan Depth, and I/O Scope

Assumption 1 (underflow and exp-accuracy).

Exponentials underflowing below the IEEE-754 single-precision subnormal range are treated as zero; the library exp satisfies |fl⁡(exp⁡(x))−exp⁡(x)|≤κ​u​exp⁡(x)|\mathrm{fl}(\exp(x))-\exp(x)|\leq\kappa\,u\,\exp(x) for all x≤0x\leq 0, for a modest constant κ\kappa independent of nn.

Lemma 1 (Bounded exponents).

With running-max rescaling mj=max⁡(mj−1,si​j)m_{j}=\max(m_{j-1},s_{ij}), we have esi​j−mj≤1e^{s_{ij}-m_{j}}\leq 1 for all terms in each prefix.

Two-level Merge Depth.

Let BB be the intra-block size (B=128B{=}128). The two-level scan induces at most

L⁡(n,B)=⌈log2⁡B⌉+2​⌈log2⁡(n/B)⌉+3≤ 2​⌈log2⁡n⌉+3\displaystyle L(n,B)=\lceil\log_{2}B\rceil+2\,\lceil\log_{2}(n/B)\rceil+3\;\leq\;2\lceil\log_{2}n\rceil+3

 (6)

merge levels along any data path.

Theorem 1 (FP32 relative error bound).

Assume IEEE-754 single precision with unit roundoff uu, finite logits, and Assumption 1. Let y^\hat{y} be the ELSA output and yy the exact output in real arithmetic.

  1. (a)

    Single query. By Higham’s (1+δ)(1{+}\delta) model [15] and Lemma 1,

    ‖y^−y‖2‖y‖2≤u​L​(n,B)+𝒪⁡(u2)≤u⁡(2​⌈log2⁡n⌉+3)+𝒪⁡(u2).\displaystyle\frac{\|\hat{y}-y\|_{2}}{\|y\|_{2}}\;\leq\;u\,L(n,B)+\mathcal{O}(u^{2})\;\leq\;u\bigl(2\lceil\log_{2}n\rceil+3\bigr)+\mathcal{O}(u^{2}).

    		 (7)
  2. (b)

    All queries (blocked). Each output row follows a path of depth ≤L⁡(n,B)\leq L(n,B); the same bound applies per row.

I/O scope.

Per query: ELSA streams K,VK,V once while updating (m,S,W)(m,S,W) and writes one yiy_{i}, attaining the Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) lower bound for reading inputs and writing the output. All queries: With tile sizes satisfying Tq​d+Tk​(d+dv)≤c​MfT_{q}d+T_{k}(d{+}d_{v})\leq cM_{f}, the DRAM traffic is

Θ⁡(n​d)+Θ⁡(n2​dTq)+Θ⁡(n2​dvTq)+Θ⁡(n​dv)\displaystyle\Theta(nd)+\Theta\!\left(\frac{n^{2}d}{T_{q}}\right)+\Theta\!\left(\frac{n^{2}d_{v}}{T_{q}}\right)+\Theta(nd_{v})

and choosing Tq≍Mf/(d+dv)T_{q}\asymp\sqrt{M_{f}/(d{+}d_{v})} yields 𝒪⁡(n2​(d+dv)/Mf)+Θ⁡(n​d+n​dv)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}(d{+}d_{v})/\sqrt{M_{f}})+\Theta(nd{+}nd_{v}), matching classical blocked I/O lower bounds up to constants; full derivations are in Supp. B.

Empirical Scaling Validation.

We measure per-head FP16 latency (median of 200 runs, single A100 GPU) for n∈{210,…,215}n\in\{2^{10},\dots,2^{15}\} tokens (Figure 3). Latency fits closely to T⁡(n)≈a​L​(n,B)+b​n2+cT(n)\approx a\,L(n,B)+b\,n^{2}+c (a=0.0142a{=}0.0142, b=1.74×10−9b{=}1.74{\times}10^{-9}, c=−0.149c{=}{-}0.149, B=128B{=}128), confirming 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log n) merge depth and 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) overall work, consistent with Theorem 1.

5 Experiments

Implementation and Experimental Setup.

We implement ELSA in Triton and CUDA C++ without HMMA/GMMA instructions, making the kernels Tensor-Core independent and deployable across GPU generations. Total arithmetic work remains 𝒪⁡(n2​d)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}d)—identical to exact attention—while the critical path is reduced to 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log n), an advantage that is most pronounced in FP32 where Tensor Core fusion is not available. Unless otherwise stated, benchmarks run on a single NVIDIA A100 (40GB, CUDA 12.6, Triton 3.2.0, PyTorch 2.6), averaged over 200 runs; Jetson TX2 and host-device offloading results are reported separately. We evaluate only exact, drop-in replacements for standard multi-head self-attention: the PyTorch Math kernel (Math), ME-SDPA in xFormers [5], FA2 [7] and FA3 [33] where applicable, and ELSA (FP32 and FP16).22 2 https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention. FA2/FA3 are evaluated in FP16/mixed precision as their FP32 kernels are not competitive on our hardware. Approximate linear-time variants [4, 40, 46] are excluded as they modify the attention operator and require retraining.

Benchmarks and Scalability on Synthetic Sequences.

We evaluate ELSA across a diverse set of tasks and models: ImageNet-1K classification [31] with ViT-B/16 [11] and Swin-T [25]; zero-shot inference with CLIP ViT-L/14 [30]; BERT sentiment on SST-2 and IMDB; and hyperspectral classification (Pavia, Salinas, WHU) with HSIMAE [41]. We benchmark single-GPU inference with random sequences of n=64n=64–16,38416{,}384 tokens in both FP16 and FP32 (Figure 4). In FP16, at the isolated kernel level, ELSA remains close to FA2/FA3 in latency at n=4,096n{=}4{,}096, with the gap further narrowing beyond n=16,384n{=}16{,}384; this kernel-only gap reverses at the full-model level (Table 3). FA2/FA3 are excluded from FP32 comparisons: their optimized paths rely on HMMA/GMMA Tensor Core instructions for FP16/BF16, and their FP32 fallback reverts to untuned SIMD execution, rendering the comparison uninformative. More broadly, FA2/FA3 require Ampere/Hopper Tensor Cores and are unavailable on older GPUs and edge devices—deployment scenarios where ELSA operates as a hardware-agnostic, FP32-exact drop-in replacement. This resolution-scalability advantage is further evidenced in Table 2, which reports attention-module-only resolution scaling (proxy scope) and should not be directly compared; extended results on 3D reconstruction models (VGGT [39] and FastVGGT [34]) are provided in Supp. G, where ELSA achieves up to 2.34×2.34\times speedup over xFormers-FP32 while matching its memory footprint.

Training and Inference on ImageNet-1K Classification.

Table 3 reports full-model FP16 forward at the same batch size (batch=8{=}8) for ViT and Swin [25] using the corrected strict FP16 scan path (no FP32 bridge, no legacy triton). We drop ME-SDPA since FA2 is the relevant FP16 flash baseline; Math-SDPA/WA are kept only as memory references. Under this strict same-batch protocol, ELSA / W-ELSA is faster than FA2 on every ViT and Swin row (∼29{\sim}29–65%65\% on ViT, ∼2{\sim}2–14%14\% on Swin), and also stays below the Math/WA memory reference on all ViT rows and on Swin-S/W16; the three remaining Swin rows incur moderate memory overhead (+3.2%{+}3.2\% to +18.6%{+}18.6\%) from short-window scan workspace, reported explicitly. Beyond inference, ELSA deploys seamlessly as a drop-in replacement during training with no modifications to the optimization pipeline. As shown in Figure 5, Swin-T, ViT-S, and ViT-T trained entirely with ELSA exhibit steady loss decay and monotonically improving top-1 accuracy, with final values within 0.1% of the corresponding Math/FA2 baseline, confirming no optimization penalty.

Downstream Tasks and LLM Inference.

Table 4 reports FP32 throughput and peak memory for HSIMAE-B/L on three hyperspectral datasets; ELSA consistently exceeds ME-SDPA in throughput while remaining within the same sub-gigabyte memory regime. For NLP workloads, Table 7 (left) reports fixed-shape bucketed BERT attention under strict FP32, where ELSA achieves 1.97×1.97\times (SST-2) and 2.27×2.27\times (IMDB) speedup over ME-SDPA; Table 7 (right) reports synthetic padding-free variable-length throughput across precision variants. To assess generality beyond vision, we evaluate ELSA on LLaMA-13B [36] under host-device offloading (Supp. H, Table 13): at long contexts (≥\geq32K tokens), ELSA delivers 17.8–20.2% throughput gains over SDPA with no retraining or weight modification; at shorter contexts (≤\leq8K), scan overhead outweighs the copy-overlap benefit.

Evaluation on Embedded Systems.

Table 6 evaluates ELSA on the resource-constrained Jetson TX2, demonstrating its hardware-agnostic nature: since ⊕\oplus requires only scalar max/exp and vector fma—with no Tensor Core or architecture-specific primitives—ELSA deploys without modification on compute capability 6.2 where FA2 provides no compatible FP32 kernel and FA3 is entirely unavailable. Across 64–900 tokens (batch 1, d=64d{=}64, FP16/FP32), ELSA consistently reduces latency by ≈35{\approx}35–38%38\% over the PyTorch Math kernel with identical memory, confirming that the scan-based efficiency advantage transfers to edge deployments. This makes ELSA particularly suited for latency-sensitive on-device inference scenarios, such as robotics and autonomous systems, where Tensor Core–dependent kernels are unavailable.

Fixed-Shape Bucketed BERT.

On BERT attention workloads with bucketed fixed-shape padding, ELSA consistently outperforms both ME-SDPA and Math-SDPA in strict FP32 (Table 7). On SST-2, ELSA achieves 1.97×\times speedup over ME-SDPA; on IMDB, 2.27×\times speedup. The larger gain on IMDB reflects its longer average sequence length, consistent with ELSA’s scan efficiency scaling with nn.

Synthetic Padding-Free Variable-Length.

Under a padding-free synthetic workload with variable-length packing (Table 7), ELSA-Strict (FP32) achieves 2.00M tok/s. ELSA-Turbo (TF32) further reaches 2.642.64M tok/s (+175.3%+175.3\%), and ELSA-FP16 peaks at 5.035.03M tok/s (+424.0%+424.0\%), demonstrating that the scan formulation’s gains compound across precision modes.

CLIP Image-Encoder Evaluation.

Table 8 reports CLIP image-encoder latency (strict FP32 and TF32-Turbo) across four ViT sizes. ELSA consistently reduces latency over ME-SDPA (see Supp. I), reaching 1.060×1.060\times at ViT-L/14@336px (strict FP32) and 1.062×1.062\times via ELSA-Turbo; per-variant details are in Supp. I. Since FA2 [8] and FA3 [33] provide no compatible FP32 path for CLIP, ELSA is the only hardware-agnostic exact-attention kernel that reduces parallel depth to O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) at full precision.

6 Discussions

Limitations.

ELSA reduces memory and I/O to O⁡(n)O(n) but preserves quadratic arithmetic complexity, and is most effective when memory rather than compute is the bottleneck. At the isolated kernel level on short sequences, scan merge overhead can leave ELSA behind FA2/FA3, though this reverses at the full-model level (Table 3); under offloading, gains of 17.8–20.2% over SDPA emerge only at ≥\geq32K tokens. The kernel is validated primarily on Ampere GPUs, and training dynamics under multi-GPU scaling remain open.

Future Directions.

Promising avenues include incorporating sparsity or low-rank structures to reduce FLOPs, extending to distributed multi-GPU training and parallelization, broadening hardware coverage beyond Ampere.

7 Conclusion

We reframe online softmax attention as a prefix scan over an associative monoid (m,S,W)(m,S,W) and present ELSA, a deployable strict FP32 exact attention kernel with a provable 𝒪⁡(u​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(u\log n) relative error bound. ELSA retains O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) arithmetic cost while reducing parallel depth to O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), uses O⁡(n)O(n) extra memory, and streams each query once, attaining the per-query Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) I/O lower bound. Requiring no Tensor Core primitives, it runs identically on A100s and Jetson TX2—a hardware-agnostic drop-in replacement for pretrained models that need neither retraining nor architectural modification. Within the strict FP32 exact-attention setting, where FA2/FA3 provide no compatible path, ELSA consistently outperforms sequential exact baselines, delivering 1.31.3–3.5×3.5\times speedups over ME-SDPA across long sequences, and also surpasses FA2 on every ViT/Swin row in the FP16 full-model same-batch regime (Table 3), making it a precise, memory-light solution for high-precision vision and language inference. Additional FP16/TF32 ablations and system-level profiling (offloading, CUDA C++ portability) are provided in the supplementary so as not to dilute the strict FP32 headline result.

A Monoid Proof for ⊕\oplus

ELSA’s parallelization strategy rests on casting online softmax attention as a parallel prefix scan over an associative operator (Sec. 4 of the main paper). This section provides the complete proof that our merge operator ⊕\oplus forms a monoid, thereby guaranteeing that any ordering of pairwise merges yields the same result—the property that makes Hillis–Steele and Blelloch scans provably correct for ELSA.

A.1 State Space and Operations

Let ℝ¯=ℝ∪{−∞}\bar{\mathbb{R}}=\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\} denote the extended reals, and let bb, hh, dd, dvd_{v} denote batch size, number of heads, key/query dimension, and value dimension respectively. Define the state space

G=ℝ¯×ℝ≥0×ℝdv,G=\bar{\mathbb{R}}\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}, (9)

whose elements are triples (m,S,W)(m,S,W): the running maximum logit mm, the normalized cumulative sum S∈ℝ≥0S\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, and the weighted value accumulator W∈ℝdvW\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}. For a=(ma,Sa,Wa)a=(m_{a},S_{a},W_{a}) and b=(mb,Sb,Wb)b=(m_{b},S_{b},W_{b}) in GG, we define two operations that underpin ⊕\oplus (Eq. (5) of the main paper).

Unnormalize:

un⁡(m,S,W)=(m,S​em,W​em)\mathrm{un}(m,S,W)\;=\;(m,\;Se^{m},\;We^{m}) (10)

exposes the raw accumulated sums prior to numerical stabilization, reversing the e−me^{-m} re-anchoring applied during the scan.

Renormalize:

renorm⁡(m,S~,W~)=(m,S~​e−m,W~​e−m)\mathrm{renorm}(m,\tilde{S},\tilde{W})\;=\;(m,\;\tilde{S}e^{-m},\;\tilde{W}e^{-m}) (11)

restores numerical stability by rescaling with the running maximum, ensuring all exponents remain ≤0\leq 0 (Lemma 1 of the main paper).

The merge operator ⊕\oplus composes two block states via un-sum-renorm:

a⊕b\displaystyle a\oplus b =renorm⁡(mc,S~a+S~b,W~a+W~b),\displaystyle=\;\mathrm{renorm}\!\left(m_{c},\;\tilde{S}_{a}+\tilde{S}_{b},\;\tilde{W}_{a}+\tilde{W}_{b}\right), (12)
mc\displaystyle m_{c} =max⁡(ma,mb),\displaystyle=\;\max(m_{a},m_{b}),

where (ma,S~a,W~a)=un⁡(a)(m_{a},\tilde{S}_{a},\tilde{W}_{a})=\mathrm{un}(a) and (mb,S~b,W~b)=un⁡(b)(m_{b},\tilde{S}_{b},\tilde{W}_{b})=\mathrm{un}(b).

A.2 Monoid Structure

Identity element.

Let 𝒆=(−∞,0,𝟎)\boldsymbol{e}=(-\infty,0,\mathbf{0}). Since un⁡(𝒆)=(−∞,0,𝟎)\mathrm{un}(\boldsymbol{e})=(-\infty,0,\mathbf{0}), by Eq. (12), 𝒆\boldsymbol{e} contributes zero to both S~\tilde{S} and W~\tilde{W}, and m=−∞m=-\infty never dominates any finite mm under max\max. Hence 𝒆\boldsymbol{e} is a two-sided identity:

a⊕𝒆=𝒆⊕a=a∀a∈G,a\oplus\boldsymbol{e}\;=\;\boldsymbol{e}\oplus a\;=\;a\hskip 18.49988pt\forall\,a\in G, (13)

which enables Blelloch’s down-sweep to initialize boundary states correctly without special-casing empty prefixes.

Associativity.

Let ua,ub,uc∈Gu_{a},u_{b},u_{c}\in G with ui=(mi,Si,Wi)u_{i}=(m_{i},S_{i},W_{i}) for i∈{a,b,c}i\in\{a,b,c\}, and let S~i=Si​emi\tilde{S}_{i}=S_{i}e^{m_{i}}, W~i=Wi​emi\tilde{W}_{i}=W_{i}e^{m_{i}} denote their unnormalized sums. For ua​b=ua⊕ubu_{ab}=u_{a}\oplus u_{b}, Eq. (12) gives ma​b=max⁡(ma,mb)m_{ab}=\max(m_{a},m_{b}) and S~a​b=S~a+S~b\tilde{S}_{ab}=\tilde{S}_{a}+\tilde{S}_{b}, W~a​b=W~a+W~b\tilde{W}_{ab}=\tilde{W}_{a}+\tilde{W}_{b}. Merging with ucu_{c} and writing m∗=max⁡(ma,mb,mc)m_{*}=\max(m_{a},m_{b},m_{c}):

S(a​b)​c=(S~a+S~b+S~c)​e−m∗,W(a​b)​c=(W~a+W~b+W~c)​e−m∗.\displaystyle S_{(ab)c}=\bigl(\tilde{S}_{a}+\tilde{S}_{b}+\tilde{S}_{c}\bigr)e^{-m_{*}},\hskip 9.24994ptW_{(ab)c}=\bigl(\tilde{W}_{a}+\tilde{W}_{b}+\tilde{W}_{c}\bigr)e^{-m_{*}}.

 (14)

The right-associative grouping ua⊕(ub⊕uc)u_{a}\oplus(u_{b}\oplus u_{c}) yields the same m∗m_{*} and the same unnormalized totals, so

Sa⁡(b​c)=(S~a+S~b+S~c)​e−m∗,Wa⁡(b​c)=(W~a+W~b+W~c)​e−m∗.\displaystyle S_{a(bc)}=\bigl(\tilde{S}_{a}+\tilde{S}_{b}+\tilde{S}_{c}\bigr)e^{-m_{*}},\hskip 9.24994ptW_{a(bc)}=\bigl(\tilde{W}_{a}+\tilde{W}_{b}+\tilde{W}_{c}\bigr)e^{-m_{*}}.

 (15)

Since Eqs. (14) and (15) are identical,

(ua⊕ub)⊕uc=ua⊕(ub⊕uc).(u_{a}\oplus u_{b})\oplus u_{c}\;=\;u_{a}\oplus(u_{b}\oplus u_{c}). (16)

Together with Eq. (13), (G,⊕,𝒆)(G,\oplus,\boldsymbol{e}) is a monoid, guaranteeing the correctness of the two-level parallel prefix scan in Sec. 4 and the FP32 error bound in Theorem 1 of the main paper. □\square

A.3 Derivation of the Floating-Point Error Bound

We derive the bound stated in Theorem 1 of the main paper. Throughout, we adopt the standard IEEE-754 model fl⁡(xopy)=(xopy)​(1+δ)\mathrm{fl}(x\mathbin{\mathrm{op}}y)=(x\mathbin{\mathrm{op}}y)(1+\delta) with |δ|≤u|\delta|\leq u (unit roundoff), and rely on Lemma 1 (bounded exponents) and Assumption 1 (exp-accuracy) from the main paper.

Per-merge error.

Consider a single pairwise merge Sout=Sa​ema−mout+Sb​emb−moutS_{\mathrm{out}}=S_{a}e^{m_{a}-m_{\mathrm{out}}}+S_{b}e^{m_{b}-m_{\mathrm{out}}}. Rounding errors arise from (1) the exponential scaling factors and (2) the subsequent addition. By Lemma 1, all scaling exponents satisfy ma−mout≤0m_{a}-m_{\mathrm{out}}\leq 0, so ema−mout∈(0,1]e^{m_{a}-m_{\mathrm{out}}}\in(0,1]—bounding the mantissa and preventing error amplification. Letting ϵk\epsilon_{k} denote the relative error at depth kk of the reduction tree, the recursive step satisfies

S^k≈Strue​(1+ϵk−1)​(1+δexp)​(1+δadd).\hat{S}_{k}\;\approx\;S_{\mathrm{true}}\,(1+\epsilon_{k-1})(1+\delta_{\mathrm{exp}})(1+\delta_{\mathrm{add}}). (17)

Dropping second-order terms 𝒪⁡(u2)\mathcal{O}(u^{2}), the error grows linearly in depth:

|ϵk|≤|ϵk−1|+c​u,|\epsilon_{k}|\;\leq\;|\epsilon_{k-1}|+c\,u, (18)

where cc counts the FLOPs per merge (one subtraction, one exponential, one multiplication, one addition).

Total depth and error bound.

The two-level scan (Sec. 4 of the main paper) contributes

L⁡(n,B)=⌈log2⁡B⌉⏟intra-block (Hillis–Steele)+2​⌈log2⁡(n/B)⌉⏟inter-block (Blelloch up/down)+const\displaystyle L(n,B)\;=\;\underbrace{\lceil\log_{2}B\rceil}_{\text{intra-block (Hillis--Steele)}}+\;\underbrace{2\lceil\log_{2}(n/B)\rceil}_{\text{inter-block (Blelloch up/down)}}+\;\mathrm{const}

 (19)

matching Eq. (6) of the main paper. Telescoping Eq. (18) over L⁡(n,B)L(n,B) levels gives

‖y^−y‖2‖y‖2≤γL⁡(n,B)≈L⁡(n,B)⋅u,\frac{\|\hat{y}-y\|_{2}}{\|y\|_{2}}\;\leq\;\gamma_{L(n,B)}\;\approx\;L(n,B)\cdot u, (20)

where γn=n​u/(1−n​u)≈n​u\gamma_{n}=nu/(1-nu)\approx nu (Higham [15]). Since L⁡(n,B)=𝒪⁡(log⁡n)L(n,B)=\mathcal{O}(\log n), the error grows logarithmically with sequence length—in contrast to naive summation (𝒪⁡(n​u)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n}\,u)) or sequential recurrence (𝒪⁡(n​u)\mathcal{O}(n\,u))—confirming the numerical stability of ELSA as n→∞n\to\infty and establishing Theorem 1.

A.4 Algorithm

This subsection provides the full pseudocode and a step-by-step walk-through of the per-query ELSA scan, which was condensed in the main paper (Sec. 4) due to space constraints. Algorithm 1 writes the scan in its sequential single-query form for clarity; the parallel two-level realization on GPU follows directly from the monoid structure of ⊕\oplus and is described in Sec. H.

State triple and invariants.

The algorithm maintains a triple (mj,Sj,Wj)(m_{j},S_{j},W_{j}) summarizing the prefix 1:j1{:}j of the key/value stream, where mjm_{j} is the running maximum logit, Sj=∑i≤jexp⁡(si−mj)S_{j}=\sum_{i\leq j}\exp(s_{i}-m_{j}) is the rescaled normalizer, and Wj=∑i≤jexp⁡(si−mj)​V​[i]W_{j}=\sum_{i\leq j}\exp(s_{i}-m_{j})\,V[i] is the rescaled weighted value sum. These three quantities together encode the exact softmax-weighted output for the prefix as Wj/SjW_{j}/S_{j}, while remaining numerically stable because all exponentials are evaluated relative to the current maximum mjm_{j}. The identity element 𝒆=(−∞,0,𝟎)\boldsymbol{e}=(-\infty,0,\mathbf{0}) initializes the recursion (Line 3) so that the first iteration encounters m0=−∞m_{0}=-\infty and immediately enters the “new max” branch.

Per-token update.

For each new token jj (Lines 4–16), the algorithm first computes the scaled inner product sj=⟨q,K⁡[j]⟩/ds_{j}=\langle q,K[j]\rangle/\sqrt{d} (Line 5). It then dispatches on whether the previous running maximum still dominates (mj−1≥sjm_{j-1}\geq s_{j}, Lines 6–10) or the new logit takes over (mj−1<sjm_{j-1}<s_{j}, Lines 11–15):

  • •

    Case A: maximum unchanged. The previous mj−1m_{j-1} is preserved as mjm_{j} (Line 7). The new contribution is folded in by computing α=exp⁡(sj−mj)\alpha=\exp(s_{j}-m_{j}) (Line 8) and adding it to both the normalizer SS and the weighted value sum WW (Lines 9–10). No rescaling of past terms is required because the normalization anchor mjm_{j} has not moved.

  • •

    Case B: new maximum. The current logit sjs_{j} becomes the new anchor (Line 12). All previously accumulated quantities are rescaled by β=exp⁡(mj−1−mj)≤1\beta=\exp(m_{j-1}-m_{j})\leq 1 (Line 13) so that they are expressed relative to the new maximum, and the contribution of token jj itself is added with weight exp⁡(0)=1\exp(0)=1 (Lines 14–15).

This conditional rescaling is precisely the online-softmax update of Eq. (2): it guarantees that, after every step, (mj,Sj,Wj)(m_{j},S_{j},W_{j}) encodes the exact softmax of the prefix without ever materializing the n×nn\times n score matrix and without floating-point overflow, since all exponentials use non-positive arguments.

Final normalization.

After processing all nn tokens, the attention output is recovered by a single division y=Wn/Sny=W_{n}/S_{n} (Line 17). Because WnW_{n} and SnS_{n} are expressed in the same exponential frame anchored at mnm_{n}, the exp⁡(⋅)\exp(\cdot) scale cancels in the ratio, yielding the exact softmax output up to floating-point round-off bounded by u​L​(n,B)u\,L(n,B) (Theorem 1 of the main paper).

From sequential to parallel.

Although Algorithm 1 is presented as a left-to-right loop for readability, its correctness depends only on the associativity of ⊕\oplus (Proposition 1), not on the order of combination. Concretely, any binary tree of ⊕\oplus-merges over the state triples u1,…,unu_{1},\dots,u_{n} produces the identical final state u1⊕⋯⊕unu_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus u_{n}. This is exactly the property exploited by the GPU implementation: intra-block reductions use a Hillis–Steele tree of depth ⌈log2⁡B⌉\lceil\log_{2}B\rceil in shared memory, and inter-block combinations use a Blelloch up-/down-sweep of depth 2​⌈log2⁡(n/B)⌉2\lceil\log_{2}(n/B)\rceil in global memory, yielding a total scan depth L⁡(n,B)L(n,B) (Sec. H). The pseudocode below should therefore be read as a specification of ⊕\oplus applied left-to-right; any parallel evaluation order matching the same monoid contract produces bit-equivalent results in exact arithmetic and bounded round-off in floating point.

B I/O Analysis and Bounds

We analyze ELSA’s I/O complexity at two levels, complementing the I/O scope paragraph in Sec. 4 of the main paper. Throughout, linear-scan refers to 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) extra memory and one-pass I/O per query; total arithmetic work remains 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}).

B.1 Per-Query Streaming

Any exact attention computation for a fixed query must read its K,VK,V inputs and write its output at least once, incurring Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) I/O. ELSA attains this lower bound by streaming KK and VV exactly once per query while keeping the running state (m,S,W)(m,S,W) in registers or fast memory—a direct consequence of the monoid structure: the identity 𝒆=(−∞,0,𝟎)\boldsymbol{e}=(-\infty,0,\mathbf{0}) allows the scan to initialize without reading any additional data.

B.2 All-Queries Tiling

For the full Q​K⊤QK^{\top} interaction and subsequent P​VPV accumulation, classical red–blue pebble arguments imply the I/O lower bound

Ω⁡(n2​(d+dv)Mf)\Omega\!\left(\frac{n^{2}(d+d_{v})}{\sqrt{M_{f}}}\right) (21)

for fast-memory capacity MfM_{f}. ELSA adopts a blocked schedule with query tile TqT_{q} and key/value tile TkT_{k} subject to

Tq​d+Tk​(d+dv)≤c​MfT_{q}d+T_{k}(d+d_{v})\;\leq\;c\,M_{f} (22)

for a small constant cc. The resulting total DRAM traffic is

Θ⁡(n​d+n​dv)+Θ⁡(n2​(d+dv)Tq).\displaystyle\Theta(nd+nd_{v})\;+\;\Theta\!\left(\frac{n^{2}(d+d_{v})}{T_{q}}\right).

 (23)

Setting Tq≍Mf/(d+dv)T_{q}\asymp\sqrt{M_{f}/(d+d_{v})} reduces this to

𝒪⁡(n2​(d+dv)Mf)+Θ⁡(n​d+n​dv),\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{n^{2}(d+d_{v})}{\sqrt{M_{f}}}\right)+\Theta(nd+nd_{v}),

 (24)

matching the lower bound (21) up to constants (Eq. (8) of the main paper). Hence linear-scan refers strictly to per-query memory (𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n)); the global all-queries schedule meets the rectangular-matrix I/O lower bound within constant factors via tiling.

C Numerical Equivalence Verification

Standard softmax attention materializes the full n×nn\times n score matrix and normalizes in a single pass—a numerically well-characterized reference implementation. Milakov and Gimelshein [27] showed that the same result can be obtained by an online procedure that maintains running statistics (mi,si,𝐰i)(m_{i},s_{i},\mathbf{w}_{i}) and updates them token by token, without ever storing the full matrix. ELSA lifts this sequential scan to a parallel prefix computation by casting those statistics as elements of an associative monoid (Sec. 4); because the merge operator ⊕\oplus is associative, any evaluation order—sequential or parallel—yields identical results in exact arithmetic. To validate this claim empirically, we use the vectorized batch formulation as a verification oracle: it computes (P^,Y^)(\hat{P},\hat{Y}) via standard matrix operations and we measure the drift against the monoid scan on GPU. In floating point the two agree to within 𝒪⁡(u​log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(u\log n) (Sec. A.3), with both sharing the same asymptotic cost—𝒪⁡(b​h​n​d)\mathcal{O}(bhnd) for the query–key product and 𝒪⁡(b​h​n​dv)\mathcal{O}(bhnd_{v}) for value accumulation.

C.1 Vectorized Reference Algorithm

Let Q,K∈ℝb×h×n×dQ,K\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times h\times n\times d} and V∈ℝb×h×n×dvV\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times h\times n\times d_{v}} denote queries, keys, and values with batch size bb, hh heads, and sequence length nn. The reference procedure computes attention probabilities P^\hat{P} and output Y^\hat{Y} as

𝐒=1d​Q​K⊤,mi=maxj𝐒:,:,i,j,E=exp⁡(𝐒−m),si=∑jE:,:,i,j,P^=E⊘s,Y^=(E​V)⊘s,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}&=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\,QK^{\top},&m_{i}&=\max_{j}\,\mathbf{S}_{:,:,i,j},\\[2.0pt] E&=\exp(\mathbf{S}-m),&s_{i}&=\textstyle\sum_{j}E_{:,:,i,j},\\[2.0pt] \hat{P}&=E\oslash s,&\hat{Y}&=(EV)\oslash s,\end{aligned}

 (25)

where ⊘\oslash denotes row-wise division. This mirrors the accumulation rules of Algorithm 1: row-wise max subtraction for stability, exponentiation, sum accumulation, and normalization. Numerical drift relative to the scan is reported in Sec. C.2.

C.2 Evaluation Results and Analysis

Metrics and Setup.

We define six complementary drift metrics on δ​P=P^−Pref\delta P=\hat{P}-P_{\mathrm{ref}} and δ​Y=Y^−Yref\delta Y=\hat{Y}-Y_{\mathrm{ref}}, chosen to probe different failure modes of a numerical reformulation:

  1. 1.

    Maximum absolute probability drift  ‖δ​P‖∞=maxb,h,i,j⁡|δ​Pb,h,i,j|\|\delta P\|_{\infty}=\max_{b,h,i,j}|\delta P_{b,h,i,j}|: worst-case pointwise error in the attention matrix—detects any single catastrophically mis-computed weight.

  2. 2.

    Relative L2L_{2} probability error  ‖δ​P‖2/‖Pref‖2\|\delta P\|_{2}/\|P_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{2}: aggregate error normalized by scale—captures global distributional shift that pointwise maxima may mask by averaging over all entries.

  3. 3.

    Mean Jensen–Shannon divergence  JSmean=1b​h​n∑b,h,iJS(P^b,h,i,:∥Pref,b,h,i,:)\mathrm{JS}_{\mathrm{mean}}=\frac{1}{bhn}\sum_{b,h,i}\mathrm{JS}(\hat{P}_{b,h,i,:}\,\|\,P_{\mathrm{ref},b,h,i,:}): per-row distributional discrepancy—JSD is symmetric and bounded, so it measures whether the shape of each query’s attention distribution is preserved, beyond individual entry magnitudes.

  4. 4.

    Argmax disagreement rate  argRate=1b​h​n∑b,h,i𝟏[argmaxjP^b,h,i,j≠argmaxjPref,b,h,i,j]\mathrm{argRate}=\frac{1}{bhn}\sum_{b,h,i}\mathbf{1}[\arg\max_{j}\hat{P}_{b,h,i,j}\neq\arg\max_{j}P_{\mathrm{ref},b,h,i,j}]: fraction of query positions where the top-attended token changes— the most behaviorally critical metric, as argmax disagreement directly alters which context the model attends to.

  5. 5.

    Maximum absolute output drift  ‖δ​Y‖∞=maxb,h,i,k⁡|δ​Yb,h,i,k|\|\delta Y\|_{\infty}=\max_{b,h,i,k}|\delta Y_{b,h,i,k}|: worst-case error in the final output embeddings propagated to the next layer—the downstream analogue of metric 1.

  6. 6.

    Relative L2L_{2} output error  ‖δ​Y‖2/‖Yref‖2\|\delta Y\|_{2}/\|Y_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{2}: normalized aggregate output error—confirms that overall output magnitude is faithfully preserved across the full tensor.

Metrics 1–4 probe the attention probability matrix PP, progressing from pointwise to distributional to functional correctness; metrics 5–6 repeat the same hierarchy for the output YY. All are computed in a fully vectorized manner on GPU; we report the median, 95th, and 99th percentiles across all tokens and heads.

Results.

Table 9 reports 95th-percentile drift between the monoid scan (FP32) and a float64 oracle reference across all scenarios. Discrepancies reach at most 3.3×10−163.3\times 10^{-16} for probabilities and 3.3×10−153.3\times 10^{-15} for outputs—well below single-precision unit roundoff u≈6×10−8u\approx 6\times 10^{-8}, confirming that the scan result is indistinguishable from the float64 reference at FP32 precision. Crucially, the argmax disagreement rate is identically zero in all scenarios, confirming that the monoid scan exactly preserves the top attention weight. Long-sequence and stress scenarios exhibit slightly larger absolute errors owing to accumulated partial sums, yet all values remain at float64-oracle-level drift—as predicted by the logarithmic depth L⁡(n,B)L(n,B) (Eq. (19)).

Figure 6 further corroborates these findings: the heatmap (left) reveals no spatial structure in |δ​P||\delta P| across token pairs—the uniformly dark field confirms that errors are random floating-point noise rather than systematic accumulation—while the log-scale histogram (right) shows |δ​Y||\delta Y| heavily concentrated near zero even under the stress scenario, with its tail bounded well below 2×10−142\times 10^{-14}, orders of magnitude beneath single-precision unit roundoff. Finally, Figure 7 directly validates monoid composition (Proposition 1) by partitioning tokens into blocks of B=128B=128, computing (m,S,W)(m,S,W) per block in parallel, and reducing via ⊕\oplus; the resulting per-block drift is indistinguishable from the float64 oracle result, confirming correctness of the associative merge at the core of ELSA.

D Ablation Studies

We examine the impact of block size (BB), accumulator precision, and resource-constrained deployment (Fig. 8). Block size B=128B{=}128 offers the best latency-occupancy trade-off across all configurations. Using FP16 for the (S,W)(S,W) accumulator causes numerical error to increase dramatically beyond 2K tokens, while FP32 remains stable throughout (Fig. 8, bottom). On Jetson TX2, baseline MHSA kernels and FA2 cannot process long sequences due to memory limitations, whereas ELSA maintains efficiency across all token lengths (Fig. 8, top).

E Variable-Length Sequence Benchmark

To ensure that performance differences are not confounded by data-layout conversions, we benchmark variable-length sequences. We generate 8 sequences with lengths uniformly sampled from [256,1792][256,1792] and compare ELSA (direct processing) against FA2 in unpadded mode (cu_seqlens), accounting for FA2’s conversion cost between padded and packed layouts.

Table 10 reports end-to-end latency, kernel time, conversion overhead, peak memory, and throughput (medians over 200 runs). ELSA’s zero-copy pipeline reduces FA2’s padded-to-packed conversion overhead (from 1.341.34 ms to 0.660.66 ms), achieving comparable end-to-end latency despite a longer kernel time.

F Window Attention and Offloading Analysis

F.1 Block Size Sensitivity

Window-ELSA introduces a block size BB controlling the work assigned to each prefix-scan step. We swept B∈{64,128,256}B\in\{64,128,256\} on Swin-T and Swin-S (A100, FP32) to characterize the throughput-memory trade-off. Smaller blocks reduce buffer pressure at the cost of more scan steps; larger blocks amortize scan overhead but may spill to slower memory. Concretely, B=64B{=}64 reduces throughput by ∼15%{\sim}15\% while cutting memory by ∼20%{\sim}20\%; B=256B{=}256 yields negligible speedup but increases memory by ∼20%{\sim}20\%. Relaxing synchronization to every two blocks saves ∼5%{\sim}5\% runtime at a cost of ∼8%{\sim}8\% extra memory. We therefore adopt B=128B{=}128 with per-block synchronization as the default operating point; memory-constrained platforms may prefer B=64B{=}64.

F.2 Offloading Performance

Methodology.

We quantify PCIe–compute overlap using LLaMA-13B instantiated as a meta-graph with no materialized weights; layer weights are loaded one layer at a time during the forward pass via asynchronous double-buffering (layer n+1n{+}1 transfers while layer nn computes). Each layer is instrumented with three CUDA event pairs measuring (i) H2D transfer time (copy_ms), (ii) kernel computation time (compute_ms), and (iii) idle time (wait_ms). We summarize overlap via

Overlapeff=1−wait_mstotal_ms,\mathrm{Overlap}_{\mathrm{eff}}=1-\frac{\texttt{wait\_ms}}{\texttt{total\_ms}}, (26)

which approaches 1.0 when PCIe transfers are fully hidden by computation.

Results.

Table 13 reports results for LLaMA-13B (FP32, batch 1) across four sequence lengths. At 4K and 8K tokens the workload is PCIe-bound: transfers complete faster than ELSA’s scan overhead, yielding higher idle time (0.727 ms and 1.005 ms vs. 0.228 ms and 0.322 ms for SDPA) and lower throughput (−-42.4% and −-25.2% respectively). At 32K tokens, ELSA’s lower memory footprint allows computation to begin earlier, reducing idle time from 540 ms to 467 ms/layer and delivering a 17.8% throughput gain (1.460 vs. 1.239 M tok/s). At 65K tokens ELSA sustains 20.2% higher throughput (0.882 vs. 0.734 M tok/s), confirming that memory efficiency compounds into end-to-end gains as sequences grow.

G On 3D Large Reconstruction Model

To validate ELSA’s effectiveness on 3D vision tasks, we evaluate it within the Visual Geometry-Grounded Transformer (VGGT) [39], a feed-forward Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) for multi-view 3D reconstruction. VGGT alternates between frame-wise and global attention layers; the global attention aggregates cross-view information but becomes the computational bottleneck as the number of frames grows.

Experimental Setup.

We compare ELSA against FA2-FP16, xFormers-FP32 (ME-SDPA), and PyTorch Math under two configurations: (1) VGGT Baseline on 50–150 frames, and (2) FastVGGT [34], a memory-optimized variant with token merging. All experiments use 350×518350\times 518 input resolution, yielding 1,041 tokens per frame (28×3728\times 37 patches plus camera and register tokens).

Results on VGGT Baseline.

Table 11 shows that ELSA-FP32 achieves a 1.46×\times speedup over xFormers at 50 frames (12.56 s vs. 18.36 s) while matching memory usage (15.74 GB, within 0.01 GB). The advantage compounds with sequence length, reaching 2.34×\times at 150 frames (55.97 s vs. 130.83 s) with an identical 37.59 GB footprint. FA2-FP16 remains the fastest baseline (3.67 s at 50 frames) but consumes 17.16 GB—9% more than ELSA-FP32.

Results on FastVGGT Scaling.

Table 12 demonstrates ELSA’s scalability on longer sequences. At 400 frames, ELSA-FP32 completes inference in 158.04 s versus xFormers’ 218.30 s (1.38×\times speedup), with identical 32.70 GB memory. The Math baseline runs out of memory beyond 30 frames due to its O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) attention matrix materialization. Across all frame counts, ELSA’s memory overhead relative to xFormers remains negligible (<<0.01 GB), confirming that the O⁡(n)O(n) auxiliary state (m,S,W)(m,S,W) imposes no practical burden at these scales.

Analysis.

ELSA’s O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) scan depth confers two key advantages for multi-view 3D reconstruction: (1) efficient parallelization over long token sequences (10K–100K tokens across views), and (2) reduced global synchronization overhead compared to xFormers’ O⁡(n/Tk)O(n/T_{k}) sequential tiling. At 400 frames with 1,041 tokens per frame (416,400 tokens total), the number of global synchronization points drops from ∼3,250{\sim}3{,}250 (xFormers, Tk=128T_{k}=128) to ∼15{\sim}15 (scan-tree depth ⌈log2(×1041/128)⌉+3≈15\lceil\log_{2}(400\!\times\!1041/128)\rceil+3\approx 15), directly explaining the observed 1.38×\times end-to-end speedup.

H CUDA C++ Backend and Portability

While our primary implementation uses Triton for rapid prototyping, we provide a CUDA C++ backend for deployments without JIT support or requiring finer control over the memory hierarchy. Both backends share the same algorithmic core—a two-level prefix scan over the monoid (m,S,W)(m,S,W)—differing only in how that scan is realized: within each block we apply a Hillis–Steele [16] or Kogge–Stone [20] scan, and across blocks a Blelloch scan [2] via cooperative groups and CUB’s BlockScan primitive [28], ensuring portability across GPU generations. Vectorization width and block size are exposed as template parameters and autotuned at runtime. Critically, the backend avoids Tensor-Core (HMMA/GMMA) instructions, enabling FP32 execution on devices such as Jetson TX2 where Tensor Cores are absent. Preliminary internal benchmarks on A100, L4, and Jetson suggest that the C++ backend remains within roughly 10–15% of the Triton implementation.

The C++ backend’s fine-grained memory control proves particularly advantageous under host-device offloading, where layer weights are streamed from CPU memory one layer at a time. Table 13 reports results for LLaMA-13B [36] (FP32, batch 1) using asynchronous double-buffering across four sequence lengths. At 4K and 8K tokens the workload is PCIe-bound: transfers complete faster than ELSA’s scan overhead, causing higher per-layer idle time (0.727 ms and 1.005 ms vs. 0.228 ms and 0.322 ms for SDPA), and SDPA holds a throughput edge (−-42.4% and −-25.2% for ELSA). At ≥\geq32K tokens, however, ELSA’s lower memory footprint allows computation to begin earlier, reducing per-layer wait from 540 ms to 467 ms and from 2069 ms to 1695 ms respectively, translating to 17.8% and 20.2% throughput gains over SDPA, confirming that ELSA’s memory efficiency compounds into end-to-end gains as sequences and transfer times grow. Table 14 further reports LLaMA-8B direct inference (no offloading), where ELSA’s throughput gain scales from ++1.7% at 4K to ++12.3% at 16K tokens.

I ELSA Variants

We examine ELSA’s performance across different precision modes, long-context workloads, and offload scenarios. Unless otherwise stated, throughput is reported in millions of tokens per second (M tok/s) and memory refers to peak GPU usage.

FP32 variants and memory trade-offs.

The main paper reports both strict FP32 and TF32-Turbo results. Strict FP32 is the primary headline for exact-attention claims; TF32-Turbo is an optional higher-throughput variant. We additionally benchmark a memory-lean variant (streaming smaller key-value chunks controlled by η\eta), which trades memory for throughput. Table 15 compares these variants against ME-SDPA at 16K tokens.

Strict FP32 achieves 3.4×3.4\times throughput improvement (1.36M vs. 0.40M tok/s) at a modest memory increase from 0.289 GB to 0.336 GB. ELSA-Turbo (TF32) delivers an additional 5% speedup (1.43M tok/s) while preserving FP32-quality outputs; numerical error remains within 10−410^{-4} relative to strict FP32. The memory-lean variant (η=0.25\eta{=}0.25) matches ME-SDPA’s 0.288 GB footprint while sustaining 0.13M tok/s. Taken together, these variants span a continuum from maximum throughput to minimal memory, allowing practitioners to select the operating point best suited to their hardware constraints.

FP16 regime and FlashAttention comparison.

At 16K tokens in FP16, ELSA delivers 2.49M tok/s with 0.19 GB memory. FlashAttention-2 [8] achieves 2.88M tok/s (∼15%{\sim}15\% faster) but requires 0.29 GB; FlashAttention-3 [33] reaches 2.73M tok/s at 0.36 GB. ME-SDPA sustains only 1.47M tok/s despite matching ELSA’s 0.19 GB footprint. Across sequence lengths, FA2 leads in raw throughput, but ELSA consistently achieves the lowest memory usage among exact kernels and narrows the speed gap as sequences grow. ELSA thus carries its long-context advantages into FP16 while remaining competitive with hardware-fused kernels.

J Limitations

Arithmetic Complexity.

ELSA eliminates the O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) memory bottleneck but preserves quadratic arithmetic complexity: the prefix-scan formulation parallelizes computation and reduces memory traffic to O⁡(n)O(n), yet still performs all pairwise interactions. The term linear-scan refers strictly to the additional memory and I/O overhead, not to arithmetic complexity; ELSA is therefore best suited to regimes where memory rather than compute is the primary bottleneck.

Short-Sequence and Window Attention.

For windowed MHSA (e.g., Swin with n≤196n\!\leq\!196), the O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) scan-depth advantage diminishes and per-level merge overhead becomes visible, while FA2/3 are highly optimized for small tiles. Table 16 shows that ELSA consistently outperforms the unfused Math baseline in both latency and memory—improving by up to 5.1% and 21.1% respectively—yet FA2 remains faster in this short-window FP16 regime. This is consistent with ELSA’s design goal: long/global contexts and FP32 portability, where fused kernels provide no compatible alternative.

Training and Multi-GPU Scaling.

The prefix-scan formulation introduces inter-block data dependencies that complicate sequence parallelism: the monoid reduction across blocks must complete before downstream layers proceed, creating synchronization barriers that do not exist in standard attention. Efficient multi-GPU scaling therefore requires careful pipeline scheduling to overlap these reductions with communication, which remains future work.

Hardware Coverage.

The current kernel is validated primarily on Ampere GPUs (A100, L4) and Jetson TX2; broader coverage across Hopper, Ada Lovelace, and non-NVIDIA accelerators is left to future work.
